title: Forty-Second Boyd
subtitle: A fighter pilot who said he could win any dogfight in forty seconds spent his life asking one question: why does the faster thinker win?

card.essence: A difficult, brilliant pilot turned a dogfight into four words — observe, orient, decide, act — and changed how armies, companies and even emergency doctors think about speed.

intention: you'll learn the story of John Boyd, use his loop to break down a split-second decision, and practise time clauses: as soon as, once, until, by the time.
warmup: Think of a moment when you had to decide very fast. What happened in your head?
In sport or games, does the fastest player usually win — or the one who reads the game best?
Are you someone who decides quickly, or someone who likes to wait for more information?

vocab.heading: A · What do they mean here? Work it out from the context
vocab.intro: Read the sentence, guess the meaning of the word in bold, then reveal.

items.sent: The two planes circled each other in a dogfight high above the clouds.
items.meaning: dogfight — a close fight between two fighter planes.

items.sent: From the cockpit, the pilot could see the whole runway.
items.meaning: cockpit — the part of a plane where the pilot sits.

items.sent: He made a wager with his friend: forty dollars if he lost.
items.meaning: wager — a bet; an agreement to pay money depending on a result.

items.sent: The new doctrine told every officer how the army should fight.
items.meaning: doctrine — the official set of beliefs and principles that guide an organisation, especially an army.

vocab.heading: B · Which word matches the meaning?
vocab.intro: The three words are: agile · maverick · opponent. Read each meaning, say the word, then reveal.

items.sent: (noun) A person who thinks and acts independently and often ignores the rules of their group.
items.meaning: maverick — “She was a maverick who never accepted “that's how we do it here”.”

items.sent: (noun) The person or team you are competing or fighting against.
items.meaning: opponent — “Her opponent in the final was the world champion.”

items.sent: (adjective) Able to move or change direction quickly and easily.
items.meaning: agile — “Small companies are often more agile than big ones.”

vocab.heading: C · Which word completes all three phrases?
vocab.intro: One missing word fits every phrase in the group. Say it, then reveal.

items.sent: ___ to change  ·  ___ quickly to a new job  ·  ___ a recipe
items.meaning: adapt — to change to suit new conditions.

items.sent: trust your ___  ·  a survival ___  ·  act on ___
items.meaning: instinct — a natural way of reacting without thinking it through.

items.sent: ___ your rivals  ·  be ___d by the enemy  ·  ___ the competition
items.meaning: outmanoeuvre — to gain an advantage over someone by moving or thinking more cleverly.

vocab_use: When do you trust your instinct, and when do you stop and think?
Is your workplace or school agile, or slow to adapt?
Do you know a maverick? Are they good to work with?

story.heading: Part 1 — The forty-second bet
paras: John Boyd was born in Erie, Pennsylvania, in 1927. He grew up poor, joined the army at seventeen, and later trained as a fighter pilot in the US Air Force. In 1953 he flew F-86 Sabre jets in the Korean War. He flew twenty-two missions, but the war ended before he ever fought an enemy plane.

After Korea, he became an instructor at the Air Force's Fighter Weapons School in Nevada, where the best pilots learned air combat. Boyd soon became famous — and a little feared. According to the legend, he made every pilot the same wager: start the dogfight with your plane in the perfect position, right behind him, and he would turn the fight around within forty seconds, or pay forty dollars. The story says he never had to pay. They called him “Forty-Second Boyd”.
Boyd was loud, rude and impossible to control — a true maverick. But he was also a brilliant thinker. He kept asking a question that others ignored: why do some pilots win?
checks: What happened in Boyd's Korean War service?
What question did Boyd keep asking?
answers: He flew 22 missions in F-86 jets but never fought an enemy plane before the war ended.
His opponent started in the perfect position behind him; Boyd bet he could turn the fight around within 40 seconds, or pay $40.
story.discuss: Can a difficult, rude person still be good for an organisation? Where is the limit?

story.heading: Part 2 — The puzzle of Korea
paras: The Korean War gave Boyd a puzzle. The American F-86 and the Soviet-built MiG-15 were similar planes; in some ways, the MiG was better — it could climb faster and fly higher. Yet American pilots reported winning the large majority of their fights. (Historians now think the official numbers were exaggerated, but the Americans probably did win more often.)

Boyd's answer was not speed in a straight line. The F-86 had a bubble-shaped cockpit, so its pilots could see more of the sky. And its controls were powered by hydraulics, so it could switch from one movement to the next more quickly. The Sabre was more agile, not faster. Its pilots could notice a change, react, and change again before the MiG could keep up.

In the 1960s, Boyd and a mathematician, Thomas Christie, turned this into a theory about how aircraft gain and lose energy in a turn. It changed how the Air Force designed and judged fighters, and it helped to shape famous jets such as the F-15 and the F-16. But Boyd was already thinking about something bigger than planes.
checks: In what ways was the MiG-15 better than the F-86?
What two features made the F-86 more agile?
Which famous planes did Boyd's energy theory help to shape?
answers: It could climb faster and fly higher.
The bubble cockpit (better view) and hydraulic controls (quicker changes of movement).
story.discuss: In your job, sport or studies, is it better to be faster — or quicker to change direction?

story.heading: Part 3 — Four words
paras: Boyd came to believe that every contest — between pilots, armies or companies — is a race through the same four steps. You observe what is happening. You orient yourself: you make sense of it, using your experience, training and culture. You decide what to do. You act. Then the situation changes, and you start again. He called it the OODA loop.

The side that goes through the loop faster, and more accurately, gets “inside” the other side's loop. By the time the opponent has understood what is happening, the situation has already changed. The opponent becomes confused and makes mistakes. Boyd believed the most important step was orient: if your picture of the world is wrong, fast decisions only take you to the wrong place faster.

Boyd never wrote a book. Instead, he gave a briefing called “Patterns of Conflict” that could last many hours, to anyone who would listen. The US Marine Corps built his ideas into its official doctrine, and he advised planners before the 1991 Gulf War. He died in 1997. Today, his loop is taught to business leaders, emergency doctors, police officers, cyber-security teams and athletes.
checks: What are the four steps of the OODA loop?
What happens when you get “inside” your opponent's loop?
Which step did Boyd think was most important, and why?
answers: The situation changes before your opponent understands it, so they become confused and make mistakes.
Orient — because if your understanding is wrong, fast decisions only lead to the wrong place faster.
story.discuss: Where in everyday life do people get stuck at “orient”?

tool_tab.lead: Four steps, round and round. The loop is not about rushing — it is about making sense of a changing situation faster and better than the problem, or the opponent, can change.
how: Observe — collect what is happening now: facts, signals, changes. What's new?
Orient — make sense of it. What does it mean, given what you know? Which of your assumptions might be wrong?
Decide — choose one action from your options.
Act — do it, then go straight back to observing: did it work? What has changed?

sort.intro: You are driving down a quiet street when a ball bounces into the road. Which step of the loop is each moment? Choose, then check.

items.text: Your brain connects the ball with a child who might run after it.
items.why: making sense of what you saw.

items.text: You see a red ball bounce into the road ahead.
You choose to brake instead of swerving.
You glance in the mirror and notice a car close behind you.
items.why: the loop starts again — new information.

items.text: You remember, from experience, that children often chase balls without looking.
items.why: using experience to understand the situation.

breaks: Speed isn't everything. A fast loop built on a wrong picture of the world leads to fast mistakes.
It sounds simpler than it is. Boyd's “orient” step was rich and complicated; many summaries reduce it to a slogan.
Not every problem is a contest. Some decisions, like choosing a career, need slow thinking, not a race.
discuss: Where in your life would a faster loop help? Where would a slower one be wiser?
How can a team get better at the “orient” step?

cousins.name: Plan–Do–Check–Act
cousins.text: A slower improvement cycle from the world of quality.

cousins.name: Kolb's Learning Cycle
cousins.text: Experience, reflect, think, try again — a loop for learning.

cousins.name: The Prisoner's Dilemma
cousins.text: Another Cold War tool — about trust instead of speed.

cousins.name: The Cynefin Framework
cousins.text: Helps you decide what kind of situation you are in before you act.

grammar.name: time clauses: as soon as, once, until, by the time
grammar.lead: The OODA loop is a sequence: one step happens, then the next. Time clauses let you say exactly when — and they follow a tense rule that many learners miss.
notes:
as soon as / once — immediately after, or after something is complete.
“I'll text you as soon as the plane lands.”  “Once you've paid, you can collect your ticket.”

until / till — up to that moment.
“Stay inside until the storm has passed.”

by the time — at or before that moment (often with a perfect tense in the main clause).
“By the time we got to the cinema, the film had started.”

before / after / when / while — the everyday time words.
“While she was cooking, the phone rang.”

The tense rule: for the future, use a present tense after these words — not will.
“I'll call you when I arrive.” (not ~~will arrive~~)  Use the present perfect to stress that something is complete: “once I have finished”.

exercises.heading: Choose the time word
exercises.intro: Write as soon as, until, by the time or while. Use each once.
items: 1. ___ the firefighters arrived, the building had already burned down.
2. Please don't open the oven ___ the timer rings.
3. ___ the pilot saw the warning light, she turned back to the airport.
4. Someone stole my bag ___ I was looking at the map.

exercises.heading: Find and fix the tense mistake
exercises.intro: Each sentence has one mistake. Write the correction.
items: 1. I'll tell you as soon as I will know the results. → ___
2. Once you will finish the test, give it to the teacher. → ___
3. By the time the police came, the thief escaped. → ___
4. We won't start until everyone will be here. → ___
answers: 3. the thief had escaped (it happened before they came)

grammar.closing: Now describe the four steps of a decision you make every day, using as soon as, once and until.

speak.intro: Put the loop to work. Choose a task, start the timer, and talk. Use the time clauses from the grammar tab.
speak.useful: “As soon as I noticed …, I …” · “Once I'd understood …, I decided to …” · “By the time I reacted, …” · “I got stuck at the orient stage because …”

tasks.label: Task 1 — A fast decision
paras: Describe a moment when you had to act quickly. Walk through it step by step: observe, orient, decide, act.

tasks.label: Task 2 — A slow loop
paras: Think of an organisation that reacts too slowly to change. Which step of the loop is its biggest problem?

tasks.label: Task 3 — Getting better
paras: Choose a skill, such as driving, a sport or teaching. How does experience make a person's loop faster?

final: Boyd was a maverick who made many enemies. Do great new ideas usually need difficult people?
A tool from air combat is now taught to doctors and business leaders. Is that a good thing, or does it make work sound like war?
Can you be too fast? Give an example where a slower loop would win.
From memory: tell Boyd's story in four sentences using as soon as, until, by the time and once.
